title: Trump v. Slaughter (2026)
summary: The Court held 6–3 that the FTC Act’s for-cause limit on removing commissioners violates Article II and overruled Humphrey’s Executor; the President may remove FTC commissioners at will.
notes:
Written from the slip opinion and the Congressional Research Service analysis; the assigned Shane & Bruff supplement is on file (added-sources/Class 11 - Slaughter Supplement.html) and its notes and questions are carried below. The same day, in Trump v. Cook, the Court treated the Federal Reserve as a distinct case and left its governors’ protection in place.

Questions the editors pose:
• Should Justice Kavanaugh have heeded Judge Kavanaugh's insights and argued for a bright-line differentiation between single-headed and multimember agencies under Article II?
• What would have been the advantages or disadvantages of giving Congress the choice between a single director removable at will and multimember leadership protected against at-will discharge?
• If historical rootedness can save a regulatory agency like the Fed from Article II challenge, why were the precedents for agency independence cited in Slaughter insufficient?
• Don't the Sinking Fund Commission, the Mint Board, the Revolutionary War Debt Commission, and even the First and Second National Banks of the United States, establish a historical tradition of creating independent administrative structures in contexts that 'require some measure of nonpartisan administration'?
• Might not equally compelling concerns counsel exceptions for agencies protecting the integrity of investment markets or the safety of nuclear energy?
• If functionalism is what is driving the Supreme Court's Federal Reserve exception, is the Court threatening to 'pass the line which circumscribes the judicial department, and to tread on legislative ground'?
• Would Perkins also cover an agency economist, statistician, epidemiologist, or other professional, whose advice may influence the making of policy, as long as they have 'no power to render a final decision on behalf of the United States unless permitted to do so by other Executive officers'?
• Do the implications of Slaughter for inferior officers depend upon whether there actually exist civil servants who exercise 'policymaking or administrative authority' but may still be considered 'inferior'? Who might such officers be?
• Would default rules allowing multimember commissions to act as long as any duly qualified members are present be good policy?
• Should there be a judicial remedy to prevent presidents from firing all of a commission's members? What would such a remedy look like?
• What if the revisionist historical work is sufficient to at least cast significant doubt on the soundness of unitarian originalism?
• Should changes in historical understanding weaken the case for stare decisis as applied to cases that relied on a questionable historical narrative to justify their outcomes?
• Does the very nature of historical investigation, which tends to surface more nuance and ambiguity than bright-line consensus, mean that courts should generally treat separation of powers disputes as political, rather than justiciable?
• Do you think Story was alarmist or prescient in his anxiety about an unlimited removal power?

sections.Parties: President Trump removed Rebecca Kelly Slaughter, a Federal Trade Commissioner, without asserting any of the statutory causes (inefficiency, neglect of duty, or malfeasance in office). Slaughter sued to keep her seat. The United States defended the removal as an exercise of the President’s Article II authority.
sections.Material Facts: The FTC Act has limited presidential removal of commissioners to the three listed causes since 1914, and Humphrey’s Executor (1935) upheld that limit. In March 2025 the President removed Slaughter for policy reasons rather than any listed cause, relying on the view that the restriction is unconstitutional. The modern Commission investigates, brings enforcement actions, adjudicates, and issues binding rules.
sections.Procedural History: Slaughter sued in the District of Columbia. The district court held the removal unlawful under Humphrey’s Executor and ordered her reinstated; the D.C. Circuit declined to stay that order. In September 2025 the Supreme Court stayed the reinstatement and granted certiorari before judgment. On June 29, 2026, it ruled for the President.
sections.Issue: Does the FTC Act’s for-cause removal restriction violate Article II’s vesting of the executive power in the President, and should Humphrey’s Executor be overruled?
sections.Holding: Yes, 6–3. The removal restriction is unconstitutional. The Chief Justice’s majority opinion held that the FTC exercises substantial executive power, that Seila Law and Collins had already reduced Humphrey’s Executor to a narrow exception, and that “if anything more is left of Humphrey’s, we overrule it.” The President may remove FTC commissioners at will.
sections.Reasoning:
The majority built on Myers, Free Enterprise Fund, Seila Law, and Collins: Article II vests the executive power in the President alone, and removal is the ordinary means of supervising the officers who exercise it. Humphrey’s Executor rested on a 1935 description of the FTC as “quasi-legislative” and “quasi-judicial”; the Court treated the modern Commission’s investigation, prosecution, adjudication, and rulemaking as executive power and declined to preserve an exception for multimember expert agencies. Justice Sotomayor’s dissent, joined by Justices Kagan and Jackson, argued that the Court had discarded ninety years of precedent and congressional design, and asked why monetary policy alone should keep its insulation.

For the course: the case ends the line that runs Myers → Humphrey’s Executor → Wiener → Morrison → Free Enterprise Fund → Seila Law, and it reframes the inferior-officer and adjudicator cases as questions about what for-cause protection, if any, survives below the principal-officer level.
sections.What the supplement adds:
The excerpt is the section 'Presidential Removal Power and the Roberts Court' from Shane and Bruff, Separation of Powers Law (5th ed. 2027, forthcoming). Four editorial notes lead up to Slaughter: Free Enterprise Fund v. PCAOB (2010), a 5-4 Roberts opinion striking two layers of for-cause protection, with Breyer's dissent; Seila Law v. CFPB (2020), another 5-4 Roberts opinion voiding for-cause protection for a single director with significant executive power, with Kagan's dissent quoted at length; Collins v. Yellen (2021), Alito extending Seila Law to the FHFA, followed by Biden's firing of SSA Commissioner Saul; and Trump v. Wilcox (2025), the stay order with its dictum setting the Federal Reserve apart. Then comes the edited opinion in Trump v. Slaughter, 609 U.S. ---- (2026): Chief Justice Roberts for the Court, Justice Gorsuch concurring, and Justice Sotomayor dissenting, joined by Kagan and Jackson. Eight notes follow: Trump v. Cook and the Fed; multimember versus single-headed agencies; other 'distinct historical traditions'; administrative adjudication; inferior officers; quorum-blocking removals; whether the Justices are competent historians; and Justice Story's warning.

The editors present the majority as resting on the unity of the executive, the Decision of 1789 and early presidential practice, Myers, and the claim that later cases had already reduced Humphrey's to its facts; if anything is left of Humphrey's, the Court overrules it under the Knick factors and dismisses congressional reliance as 'adverse possession.' The FTC's rulemaking, in-house adjudication and civil enforcement are all executive power, so Slaughter was the President's subordinate. The Court reserves the Federal Reserve and non-Article III judges. Gorsuch agrees but warns that the fourth branch's legislative and judicial powers have been reassigned to the President ('now the house is white') and that the Court must use its separation-of-powers doctrines. The editors stress Sotomayor's answer: the text is silent on removal, English and state practice allowed limits, the Decision of 1789 settled only that the Senate need not consent, the First Congress created semi-independent bodies, Myers is 'a castle built on sand,' 140 years of practice since the ICC deserve weight, and stare decisis alone should have decided the case. Note 7 adds that even Prakash doubts the majority's reading of 1789.

Facts stated: Trump fired Commissioners Rebecca Slaughter and Alvaro Bedoya in March 2025 without asserting statutory cause; the lower courts ruled for Slaughter; the Court stayed the order, granted certiorari before judgment, and reversed. The dissent refers to 'the six Justices in the majority.' Trump v. Cook, 146 S. Ct. 2234 (2026), decided the same day, denied a stay 5-4 (Roberts writing; Kavanaugh and Jackson concurring; Thomas, Alito with Gorsuch, and Barrett dissenting), held Fed removals reviewable, required a hearing, and set a 'substantial threshold' for cause.

topics.lrs-s-removal: Overrules Humphrey’s Executor: for-cause protection for FTC commissioners is unconstitutional.
topics.lrs-s-agency-independence: Removal protection for a multimember expert commission no longer insulates the agency from at-will removal.
topics.lrs-s-ftc-tenure: The FTC Act removal provision upheld in Humphrey's Executor is the provision held unconstitutional in Slaughter.

learning.separateOpinions: The excerpt states no numerical tally for Slaughter. It gives the opinions as: 'Chief Justice ROBERTS delivered the opinion of the Court'; 'Justice GORSUCH, concurring'; and 'Justice SOTOMAYOR, with whom Justice KAGAN and Justice JACKSON join, dissenting.' The dissent refers to 'the six Justices in the majority.' Editorial note 3 attributes a quoted 'Slaughter concurrence' to Justice Kavanaugh but cites the passage to Trump v. Cook, 146 S. Ct. 2234, 2257 (2026) (Kavanaugh, J., concurring). Related votes as the excerpt states them: Free Enterprise Fund, 5-4, Chief Justice Roberts, Breyer dissenting; Seila Law, 5-4, Chief Justice Roberts, Thomas concurring with Gorsuch, Kagan dissenting for herself, Ginsburg, Breyer and Sotomayor; Collins v. Yellen, Justice Alito for the Seila Law majority plus Justice Barrett, Sotomayor and Breyer dissenting from the constitutional holding; Trump v. Wilcox, stay granted over the dissent of the Court's three liberal Justices; Trump v. Cook, stay denied 5-4, Chief Justice Roberts for the majority, Kavanaugh and Jackson concurring, Thomas in a sole dissent, Alito dissenting for himself and Gorsuch, Barrett dissenting.
learning.why: Slaughter is the current rule on presidential removal of FTC commissioners and the reason Humphrey’s Executor is now history rather than doctrine.
